name: Battle of Marignano
info: Francis I of France, with German landsknechts and late-arriving Venetian allies, defeated the Swiss Confederacy near Melegnano, south-east of Milan, in September 1515; the Perpetual Peace of 1516 followed.

facts.place: Near the town now called Melegnano, 16 km south-east of Milan, in Lombardy, Italy, on a plain of vineyards, fields, orchards and pastures near San Giuliano
facts.sides: France under Francis I, with German landsknechts and Venetian allies under Bartolomeo d'Alviano who arrived in the morning of the second day; the Swiss, about 22,000 men, almost all pike infantry with fewer than a dozen guns. The Swiss were heavily outnumbered and outgunned.
facts.outcome: A French victory: the Swiss withdrew in good order, the French regained Milan, and the Treaty of Fribourg of 1516 ended Swiss claims to the protectorate of Milan.

t: The Swiss, about 22,000 strong and almost all pikemen, charged the French guns twice, on the evening of 13 September and the morning of 14 September, and were held by massed cannon fire and cavalry charges.
The battle hung in the balance until the Venetian forces under Bartolomeo d'Alviano arrived in the mid-morning, after which the Swiss withdrew in a single large open square.
The Treaty of Fribourg of 1516, the Perpetual Peace, lasted until the French Revolutionary Wars and opened three centuries of close ties between the Swiss Confederacy and France.
dyk: Francis I had a medal struck with the words 'I have vanquished those whom only Caesar vanquished', and asked to be knighted on the battlefield by the Chevalier Bayard.
ev: The Swiss win at Novara, take control of Milan and restore Maximilian Sforza as duke
Francis I leads his army over the Col d'Argentière, and the French capture the papal commander Prospero Colonna at Villafranca
Swiss columns of about 22,000 leave Milan and meet the French at Marignano, where the fighting lasts into the night
The Swiss attack again in the morning, and the arrival of the Venetians turns the battle against them
Francis meets Pope Leo X at Bologna, and the two agree the terms of a concordat
The Treaty of Fribourg, the Perpetual Peace, is signed between Francis and the Swiss cantons
France and the Swiss Confederacy conclude a service pact that makes Swiss regiments a regular part of the French armed forces

sections.background:
The campaign of Marignano followed years of Swiss successes, during which French fortunes in northern Italy had suffered greatly. The Swiss had taken control of Milan after their victory at the Battle of Novara in 1513 and returned Maximilian Sforza, son of Ludovico Sforza, to the ducal throne, making Milan a protectorate of Switzerland. For France, Milan was the gateway to Italy.

The prologue to the battle was an Alpine passage, in which Francis I, the newly crowned King of France, hauled 72 cannons over new-made roads across the Col d'Argentière, a previously unknown route. At Villafranca the French, led by Jacques de la Palice, captured the papal commander Prospero Colonna in a cavalry raid deep behind the allied lines, with the Chevalier Bayard providing the impetus and expertise. They also took a great deal of booty, including 600 horses.

The capture of Colonna and the sudden appearance of the French army on the plains of Piedmont stunned the allies. The Pope and the Swiss both sought terms with Francis, while the Spanish allies on their way from Naples halted to await developments. The main Swiss army retreated to Milan, and a large faction, tired of the war and eager to go home with the booty of years of campaigning, urged terms with the French.
sections.forces:
A peace agreement that gave Milan back to the French led large parts of the Swiss army to go home, but fresh troops arrived from cantons that refused to abide by the treaty. Discord swept through the Swiss forces until Matthäus Schiner, cardinal of Sion and an enemy of Francis, tricked them into battle against a far superior force by exaggerating the extent of a minor skirmish. The Swiss left Milan in disciplined columns, numbering around 22,000. They consisted almost entirely of pike infantry, fielded fewer than a dozen artillery pieces and had no cavalry.

The French were not expecting battle, since a treaty had been signed. Francis was in his tent, trying on a new suit of armour, when scouts reported the Swiss. The army formed in three divisions. The vanguard, under Charles III, Duke of Bourbon, and Marshal Gian Giacomo Trivulzio, held two shallow rises near San Giuliano, with crossbowmen behind earthworks and pavise shields on the left, a large square of landsknecht infantry in the centre and arquebusiers on the right, covering the artillery, which stood in a crescent along the south-eastern and eastern edges.

Two kilometres behind, Francis led the cavalry and 6,000 landsknechts recruited from the Netherlands, known as the Black Band of Gueldern. A kilometre further back the rearguard was led by the king's brother-in-law Charles IV, Duke of Alençon. The French had a good mix of pikemen, arquebusiers and cavalry. The Swiss, trusting to experience that a rapid advance would sweep all before them, approached in three dense masses of pikemen.
sections.course:
Close to sunset the Swiss advanced, and a forlorn hope detached from their vanguard charged the grand battery in front of the king's position with lowered pikes, intending to overrun the cannon and turn them on their owners. At first the attack drove back the landsknecht defenders and took a few guns, the speed of the advance making the French fire ineffective. Bourbon's cavalry then counter-attacked from the French right and drove the forlorn hope back to the shelter of the Swiss vanguard. The pursuing French horse took heavy losses and fell back a full kilometre.

Smoke and night hid the fighting, and in the moonlight and confusion the outcome hung in the balance. French cavalry charges, often led by the king himself with Bayard at his side, threw back temporary Swiss gains time and again. Many leading French commanders were wounded or killed, among them the Prince of Tallemont, son of Louis II de la Trémoille, who died with sixty-two wounds. Bayard cut his way through the Swiss phalanx to rescue the Duke of Lorraine. In the darkest hours both armies stopped and reorganised, and some Swiss soldiers, even whole units, slipped away.

The battle began again in the morning. The grand battery had been reassembled, and the Swiss reformed their largest phalanx and again charged the guns. Massed cannon fire at point-blank range stopped them, though they closed up and pushed on, and a cavalry charge led by Bayard forced them to give ground. They turned against Alençon's division on the left and were thrown back there too. Only the arrival in mid-morning of the Venetians under Bartolomeo d'Alviano turned the tide. The Swiss gave ground and withdrew, forming a single gigantic open square and keeping extraordinary discipline.
sections.aftermath:
The retreating Swiss army kept control of Bellinzona and the adjacent valleys of upper Lombardy, leaving a rearguard to hold them. Francis gained the city of Milan and, more importantly, the Castello Sforzesco within it, the strategic key to control of Lombardy. Maximilian Sforza, the Swiss mercenaries and the cardinal-bishop of Sion had retreated there, and submitted only when French sappers had placed mines under the foundations. Maximilian went into exile with a French purse of 100,000 écus.

After lengthy negotiations a peace was signed at Fribourg on 29 November 1516 between the Thirteen Cantons and their allies and Francis, as both King of France and Duke of Milan. In this Treaty of Fribourg, the Perpetual Peace, the Swiss Confederacy gave up all claims to the protectorate of Milan, and France paid 700,000 gold crowns in compensation. Each side agreed not to support the other's enemies, apart from existing treaties, and to arbitrate future disputes. France offered another 300,000 crowns if the Swiss would yield their transmontane territories, except Bellinzona, but this was declined. The treaty gave the Swiss trade privileges in Milan and Lyon, and only the Ossola valley went back to Milan.

On 11 December 1515 Francis met Pope Leo X in Bologna, where it was agreed that he would renounce the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges and the pope would accept his demands on the choice of French bishops. The concordat was signed by Leo X on 15 August 1516. Leonardo da Vinci, also at Bologna, was persuaded to go to France, where Francis gave him the Clos Lucé manor and a pension of 7,000 scudi.
sections.sources:
The battle is known partly through the words of those who took part. Francis I reported to his mother that thirty brave charges had been hurled by the French gendarmerie against the stubborn Swiss, a boast that shows how he wished the fighting to be seen. He also ordered the medal that claimed a victory over those whom only Caesar had vanquished. Marshal Trivulzio, a veteran of every war for the previous 40 years, called it the battle of giants and said that all earlier battles of his lifetime had been child's sport.

How to weigh the victory is disputed. It could be called the expected result, since the Swiss were heavily outnumbered and outgunned, but the Swiss had often won from such positions and the French victory did not come easily. The immediate causes of the Swiss defeat are given as their failure to take the French artillery early and the arrival of the Venetians, with a weak command structure behind them: earlier in 1515 the Swiss diet had let each captain decide whether his company would go on or retreat. Swiss historiography has also tended to credit a lesson learned at Marignano with the end of Swiss offensive wars, though the later division of the Reformation and defeats at Bicocca, Sesia and Pavia were at least as effective.
sections.legacy:
The battle ended all Swiss aspirations in Milan. The Swiss Confederacy never again fought France or Milan, did not go to war against anyone after 1525, and apart from Bern's conquest of Vaud in 1536, acting on its own, launched no further offensive against an external enemy. The Perpetual Peace was kept for the rest of the lifetime of the Kingdom of France and was broken only when the French Republic invaded Switzerland in 1798. It opened three centuries of close ties between the Confederacy and France, while Switzerland moved away from its association with the Holy Roman Empire. The service pact of 1521 made Swiss mercenary regiments a regular part of the French armed forces. The arrangement outlasted three centuries, with four Swiss regiments in Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812, until foreign military service of Swiss citizens was outlawed in 1848.

French success at Marignano eventually galvanised opposition in the divided peninsula and turned the European balance of power against Francis I. Huldrych Zwingli, present at the battle as church patron at Glarus, blamed Cardinal Schiner's warmongering for the disaster, became an outspoken opponent of mercenary service and began to preach against the high clergy, the first signs of the radicalisation that led to the Swiss Reformation.

The battle is commemorated by Pierre Bontemps's bas-relief on Francis I's tomb at Saint-Denis, a painting by Antoine Caron for Fontainebleau, now in the National Gallery of Canada, and Clément Janequin's chanson La guerre. The Swiss hero Hans Bär appears in a fresco on the tower of the Basel City Hall, and Jean Daetwyler's march Marignan of 1939 is the official orchestral hymn of the canton of Valais.

summary: At Marignano on 13 and 14 September 1515 Francis I's French army, with landsknechts and Venetian allies, beat back a Swiss force of about 22,000 that had charged its guns. The Swiss gave up Milan in the Perpetual Peace of 1516, and close ties with France followed.
references: Michael Mallett, The Italian Wars, 1494-1559 (Pearson Education Limited, 2012)
R.J. Knecht, Francis I (Cambridge University Press, 1984)
notes: The article gives no strength for the French or Venetians, only 'far superior' and 'heavily outnumbered and outgunned'; none is given in the text.
The article says the French vanguard had crossbowmen on the left and arquebusiers on the right, but also that Bourbon's cavalry counter-attacked 'from the French right'; both kept as written.
'Black Band of Gueldern' later appears as 'Black Legion' in the article; I used the first name only.

Left out: the quotation 'dulce bellum inexpertis' and Zwingli's move to Einsiedeln and Zürich (length); the Gaul-style detail of Janequin's piece. Sources section is largely the participants' statements and the article's historiographical comments, as the article names no chronicler of the battle.
The article's 'daring cavalry raid' and 'bloody shambles' left out as colour; 'decisive French victory' is the article's own phrase, used only in the summary of outcome as 'victory'.
